Chapter 6: The Locked Door—Why We Can’t Always Explain Our Instincts
Have you ever had someone ask, “Why did you do that?” And you just... don’t really know? Sometimes, the answer’s obvious. But more often, the real reason sits just out of reach—almost like it’s behind a locked door in your mind.
Think about it: We act, we speak, we decide—sometimes in a split second. But when we try to explain ourselves, the words just don’t fit. It’s not that we forgot. It’s just that so much of our thinking happens deep below the surface.
Imagine a tennis coach watching a player serve. In an instant, the coach senses something’s off. But if you ask for details? Well, the coach might give a technical answer, but really, it’s just a guess. The real spark—the thing that triggered their reaction—is buried beneath years of experience and gut feeling. It’s like there’s a secret workshop in the mind, quietly making judgments before we even realize.
That hidden process? The author calls it the “locked door.” Most of what drives our snap judgments never actually makes it to the surface. We invent reasons after the fact, trying to make sense of choices we made in a heartbeat. It’s not that we’re lying—it’s just the mind’s way of filling in the blanks.
There’s a great experiment where people had to pick between two almost identical paintings. When asked why they chose one, they struggled, offering reasons that just didn’t match their real feelings. The truth? Their choice happened in a blink, shaped by little cues they couldn’t even name. The explanations came later, built out of what sounded reasonable.
Now, that gap between what we do and why we say we did it—it can feel a bit unsettling, can’t it? It means that even the answers we’re most confident about might just be stories, not facts. But here’s the upside: It shows just how deep our intuition goes. Our minds are always working, always learning, even when we don’t notice.
Most of the time, this hidden process is actually a gift. It lets us move through the world quickly and confidently, making sense of complicated stuff without getting stuck. But it also means our self-knowledge has its limits. The reasons we give for our choices are often just our best guesses.
So, here’s something important: The locked door isn’t a flaw—it’s a feature. It protects us from getting overwhelmed, and lets our minds work quietly in the background. Sometimes, the real challenge is just accepting that not everything can be explained. And maybe, every now and then, the best answers are the ones we can’t quite put into words.
